title: A high-entropy form of $R$Mn$_6$Sn$_6$ with distinct magnetotransport regimes correlated to different magnetic structures
authors: Kyle W. Fruhling, Jonathan Gaudet, William D. Ratcliff, Jonathan S. White, Siddharth Nandanwar, Noah J. Fau, Gregory T. McCandless, Enrique O. González Delgado, Julia Y. Chan, Oksana Zaharko, Michael A. Susner, Fazel Tafti
abstract: The kagome $R$Mn$_6$Sn$_6$ material family has attracted significant attention as high-temperature metallic magnets with a host of different magnetic orderings and anisotropy. Theoretical studies point to the rare-earth ($R$) as the determining factor for both the direction of magnetic anisotropy and the type of magnetic ordering in a given compound. This motivates studying high-entropy forms of $R$Mn$_6$Sn$_6$ to examine how the interplay of several rare-earth elements leads to different magnetic states in a single crystal. Here, we present a rare-earth mix of Tb, Dy, Ho, Er, Tm, and Lu that produces phase transitions from a paramagnet to an easy-plane ferrimagnet (FiM) below $T_{\text{C}}$ = 380 K, then to a FiM easy-axis state at $T_{\text{SR1}}$ = 207 K, to a canted FiM ground state below $T_{\text{SR2}}$ = 79 K. This behavior is consistent with previously reported high-entropy $R$Mn$_6$Sn$_6$ compounds; however, uniquely, the rare-earth mix studied here exhibits a broad transition from easy-plane to easy-axis anisotropy from 270 K to 170 K, and reveals a nonmonotonic magnetoresistance. Using neutron scattering data, we found that both observations correlate with an incommensurate modulated contribution to the spin state due to competing rare-earth interactions. This magnetoresistive behavior and the correlated spin structures underscore the potential for rare-earth engineering of magnetism.
summary: This work investigates a high-entropy rare-earth manganite, $	ext{RMn}_6	ext{Sn}_6$, to understand how mixing multiple rare-earth elements controls its magnetic state. Through extensive measurements, the authors map out multiple magnetic transitions and observe a correlation between the magnetotransport anomalies and an incommensurate spin modulation. This highlights the potential for rare-earth engineering in designing novel magnetic materials.
main_problem: To investigate how the interplay of multiple rare-earth elements in a high-entropy $	ext{RMn}_6	ext{Sn}_6$ structure influences its magnetic ordering and magnetotransport properties.
main_result: The material exhibits complex, temperature-dependent magnetic transitions (Paramagnet $	o$ easy-plane $	o$ easy-axis $	o$ canted $	ext{FiM}$) correlated with an incommensurate modulated spin state and nonmonotonic magnetoresistance.
method: The study combines multiple experimental techniques, including magnetization measurements (MPMS), electrical transport (Hall effect, MR), and advanced neutron scattering (SANS, single-crystal diffraction).
model_or_system: The physical system is the high-entropy compound $	ext{HE}166 = (	ext{Tb},	ext{Dy},	ext{Ho},	ext{Er},	ext{Tm},	ext{Lu})_1	ext{Mn}_6	ext{Sn}_6$, which is a layered magnet whose magnetism is governed by competing rare-earth interactions.
key_observables: Magnetic transition temperatures ($T_C=380 	ext{ K}$, $T_{	ext{SR}1}=207 	ext{ K}$, $T_{	ext{SR}2}=79 	ext{ K}$), magnetoresistance ($	ext{MR}$), and incommensurate magnetic scattering peaks ($\mathbf{k}_{	ext{inc}}$).
important_parameters: The rare-earth mixing ratio and the temperature/field regimes defining the magnetic anisotropy transitions (e.g., $270 	ext{ K}$ to $170 	ext{ K}$ for easy-plane to easy-axis change).
main_assumptions: The magnetic behavior is assumed to be dictated by the interplay of various magnetic couplings ($J_1, J_2, J_3, J_{	ext{R-Mn}}$) and the rare-earth mixing effects.
figures_summary: Figures detail magnetization curves, magnetoresistance vs. field plots, and neutron scattering data showing both commensurate and incommensurate magnetic reflections at various temperatures.
paper_structure: The paper systematically characterizes the material's structure (XRD, EDX), maps out its magnetic phase transitions using magnetization measurements, and correlates these magnetic changes with transport anomalies (MR, Hall effect) and structural probes (Neutron Scattering).
why_interesting: The study demonstrates how engineering disorder (high-entropy mixing) can stabilize and reveal complex, multi-stage magnetic ground states and associated transport phenomena, which is a key area of modern condensed matter physics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. (a) The crystal structure of HE166 (same as other RMn6Sn6) showing the mixed rare-earth site and the kagome Mn layer. (b) Magnetic couplings in the RMn6Sn6 structure. (c) Magnetic ground states of various RMn6Sn6 materials in their pure form containing the rare-earth elements that were used to produce HE166. The blue arrows represent the rare-earth moment of a given unit cell and the orange arrows represent the Mn moments in a unit cell. (d) DC susceptibility vs. temperature measured in HE166. Inset: Example image of a hexagonal HE166 crystal on millimeter paper.

FIG. 2. Magnetization as a function of field measured in HE166 at (a) 2 K, (b) 150 K (inset: derivative of magne- tization with respect to field with H∥a), (c) 210 K (inset: derivative of magnetization with respect to field with H∥c), and (d) 350 K. The background color of each panel corre- sponds to the temperature regimes in Fig. 1d.

FIG. 3. Longitudinal magnetoresistance as a function of field for HE166 at (a) 20 K, (b) 150 K, (c) 210 K, and (d) 350 K. The background color of each panel corresponds to the temperature regimes in Fig. 1d. All four panels show in-plane resistivity data, measured under both in-plane field (blue line) and out-of-plane field (orange line).

FIG. 4. (a) SANS intensity at 210 K and zero-field. The white solid box highlights the region near the beam stop inte- grated in order to estimate the ferromagnetic in-plane contri- bution, and the white dotted box highlights the incommen- surate peak. (b) Neutron high-angle diffraction intensity in zero-field around the (002) nuclear peak. Incommensurate satellite peaks appear between 170 K and 270 K. (c) Left axis: the relative intensity of three different scattering pro- cesses; the in-plane FM contribution of the Q∼0 integration region (blue circles) as shown in the solid box in (a), its out- of-plane contribution (black squares), and the intensity of the satellite peak (red triangles)...

FIG. 5. (a) Left axis: Satellite peak intensity at 220 K as a function of field showing complete suppression by 0.2 T. Right axis: Magnetoresistance at 220 K showing a change of slope at the same field where the satellite intensity is suppressed.
